profile.summary: ESM-1b is a protein language model from Meta's FAIR protein team. It reads a single amino-acid sequence and was trained without labels to predict masked amino acids from their context. Its per-residue and per-sequence representations are used as features for structure and function prediction, and its masked-token scores can be used to score the effect of sequence variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: introduction, Model description; paper: abstract

summary_quotes.text: is a transformer protein language model, trained on protein sequence data without label supervision.
the model is trained to predict amino acids from the surrounding sequence context
The learned representations can be used as features for downstream tasks.
found that ESM-1b can be used to score the effect of sequence variations on protein function.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESM-1b is a 33-layer transformer based on the RoBERTa architecture, with pre-activation layer normalisation. It was trained with the masked language modelling objective: 15% of amino acids are masked and the model predicts them from the rest of the sequence. The training data are raw protein sequences only, with no structure or function labels. The authors found the hyperparameters by a search on 100M-parameter models and scaled them to a model of about 650M parameters trained on UniRef50 representative sequences (UR50/S). The representations can be read out per residue or averaged per sequence, and the attention maps give unsupervised contact predictions.

quotes.text: The ESM-1b model is based on the [RoBERTa](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.11692) architecture and training procedure
One architecture difference from the RoBERTa model is that ESM-1b uses [pre-activation layer normalization]
15% of the amino acids are masked.
The training is purely unsupervised -- during training no labels are given related to structure or function.
We scale the hyperparameters identified by this search to train a model with ∼650 M parameters (33 layers) on the UR50/S dataset, resulting in the ESM-1b Transformer.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one ESM-1b checkpoint, esm1b_t33_650M_UR50S, released with the Rives et al. paper in a December 2020 update. It is distributed as a PyTorch file through the fair-esm package and as a Hugging Face transformers checkpoint at biohub/esm1b_t33_650M_UR50S. The earlier ESM-1 checkpoints and the later ESM-1v and ESM-2 models are separate models. The model card says ESM-2 will usually perform better and recommends it unless the goal is to compare against ESM-1b. A result should name the checkpoint and, for Hugging Face use, the revision; this page read revision 7b37824b.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Transformer protein language model trained with masked language modelling on single sequences, without labels.

quotes.text: is a transformer protein language model, trained on protein sequence data without label supervision.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: RoBERTa-style transformer with pre-activation layer normalisation: 33 layers, hidden size 1280, 20 attention heads, feed-forward size 5120.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: An amino-acid sequence, uppercased and tokenised one residue per token, with a <cls> token at the start. Masked positions use a <mask> token.

quotes.text: The protein sequences are uppercased and tokenized using a single space and a vocabulary size of 21.
the masked amino acids are replaced by `<mask>`

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Per-residue representations from any layer, per-sequence representations by averaging, amino-acid predictions at masked positions, and unsupervised contact maps from attention.
facts.source_locator: README: Getting started with this repo; Compute embeddings in bulk from FASTA

quotes.text: `per_tok` includes the full sequence, with an embedding per amino acid (seq_len x hidden_dim).
`mean` includes the embeddings averaged over the full sequence, per layer.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: 650M (esm1b_t33_650M_UR50S), as listed in the repository; the paper says about 650M. No exact count is published in the sources read.
facts.source_locator: README: Pre-trained Models; paper: ESM-1b Transformer

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: UniRef50 release 2018_03 representative sequences (the UR50/S dataset), about 30 million sequences according to the model card. The paper's 250 million sequences describe the largest UniParc dataset it explored, not the ESM-1b training set.

the high-diversity sparse dataset (UR50/S) uses the UniRef50 representative sequences

run_guide.summary: Install the fair-esm package, load the ESM-1b checkpoint and extract per-residue and per-sequence representations for one protein.
prerequisites: A CUDA device is optional for the repository's extraction script; the README's Python example runs on CPU.
Code and weights are MIT licensed. The weights (about 650M parameters) are downloaded automatically to ~/.cache/torch/hub/checkpoints.

steps.title: Load ESM-1b and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import esm

model, alphabet = esm.pretrained.esm1b_t33_650M_UR50S()
batch_converter = alphabet.get_batch_converter()
model.eval()  # disables dropout for deterministic results

data = [
    ("protein1", "MKTVRQERLKSIVRILERSKEPVSGAQLAEELSVSRQVIVQDIAYLRSLGYNIVATPRGYVLAGG"),
]
batch_labels, batch_strs, batch_tokens = batch_converter(data)
batch_lens = (batch_tokens != alphabet.padding_idx).sum(1)

with torch.no_grad():
    results = model(batch_tokens, repr_layers=[33], return_contacts=True)
token_representations = results["representations"][33]

sequence_representations = []
for i, tokens_len in enumerate(batch_lens):
    sequence_representations.append(token_representations[i, 1 : tokens_len - 1].mean(0))
PY
steps.explanation: The README's quick-start example, wrapped in a shell heredoc, with the ESM-2 loader replaced by the ESM-1b loader named in the README's model table, one input sequence kept, and the plotting lines removed. ESM-1b has 33 layers, so layer 33 is the final layer as in the README example.
